opening_message:
Ticket 1: Keith Mclaughlin (employee ID E032) requests write access to Source Code.

Team memory: 2 note(s) about employee E032.
Note 1 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: full_time
  - recommendation for Source Code: write
  - comment: Keith Mclaughlin (E032), Analyst, full-time employee, requests write access to Source Code. Full-time employees may have up to write access (admin requires owning role; Analyst does not own Source Code). Requested level is within policy, so recommend write.
Note 2 (ticket 1):
  - role: Analyst
  - employment type: contractor
  - security training: basic
  - recommendation for Source Code: read
  - comment: Security DB shows E032 is a contractor with basic security training (HR note listed full-time; Security DB is authoritative here). Contractors with basic training max out at read; write requires advanced training. Recommend read.
reason: The Security DB (authoritative) identifies E032 as a contractor with basic security training. Per policy, contractors with basic training may have at most read access (write requires advanced training). The requested write level exceeds the maximum, so the maximum (read) is granted.

content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee E032 (Keith Mclaughlin) requests write access to Source Code.

There are two notes with conflicting information:
- Note 1 (HR): role Analyst, employment type full_time, recommendation for Source Code: write
- Note 2 (Security): role Analyst, employment type contractor, security training basic, recommendation: read. Security DB is authoritative per the note.

The Security note says the HR note listed full-time but Security DB is authoritative, showing contractor with basic training.

So employment type: contractor, security training: basic.

Policy for contractors: read, or write if they have advanced security training. Never admin.

Since contractor with basic training, max is read. Requested write is above max, so grant max = read.

Decision: read.
